## Annotation and Interpretation

At this point the EWAS is done: we have a per-CpG table of effect sizes and
p-values, BACON-adjusted for residual inflation (notebook
[06](06_ewas.qmd)), and — if we chose the stratified route — a METAL
meta-analysis of the strata (notebook [07](07_pipeline.qmd)). Next we introduce 
functional annotation and region-level analysis. Previously it was mentioned that
the snakemake pipeline can do differentially methylated region analysis in addition 
to the EWAS. But, it wasn't really explained what that is or why you would want to 
do it. Here we more fully detail functional annotation and secondary analysis (including 
regional analyses) that are a necessary part in interpretation of results.

1. **CpG-level functional annotation** — attach genomic coordinates, gene
   context, CpG-island relationship, and expression links
   to every probe, so the top hits can be read as *"this CpG sits in the
   promoter of gene X"* rather than *"cg16340178"*.
2. **Region-level analysis (DMRs)** — ask whether *spatially clustered* CpGs
   move together. A differentially methylated region (DMR) can be highly
   significant even when no single CpG in it survives genome-wide correction,
   because neighboring probes are correlated and that correlation carries
   signal [@pedersen2012combp; @peters2015dmrcate].

For functional annotation of the EWAS results we use Wanding Zhou's hg38 EPIC annotation resources 
[@zhou2017comprehensive]. Zhou recently (July of 2026) made a major update of his website and 
released new versions of his resources (v8.1). This tutorial implements some of the newest version of Zhou's 
files in addition to some 'legacy' files. The Snakemake pipeline uses entirely legacy files at the moment, 
but will be updated to use the latest versions in the next release. 
Most of the annotation in this chapter is hg38, but not all of it. The enrichment tools
`goregion`, `gometh` and `methylGSA` default to Illumina's hg19 annotation package; here
we pass each of them Zhou's hg38 annotation instead, but the knowYourCG knowledgebases
and the web tools still rest partly or wholly on hg19. The table below lists the build and source behind each section. It matters
most where the chapter compares tools, because two tools built on different annotations
are not a like-for-like comparison. For tools that take probe IDs rather than
coordinates, the build shows up in *which genes or features each probe was assigned
to*, not in any coordinate you see.

| Section | Tool | Genome build | Annotation source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Part 1: gene and CpG-island context | Zhou manifests | hg38 | Zhou, GENCODE v41 and v36 |
| Part 1: eQTM layer | BIOS cis-eQTM catalog | hg19 (original mapping; joined by probe ID) | BIOS consortium, gene symbols re-mapped to current HGNC |
| Part 2: region calling | comb-p, `ENmix::combp` | hg38 | Zhou coordinates |
| Part 2: annotating the DMR | overlap with UCSC tables | hg38 | UCSC refGene, cpgIslandExt, HGNC |
| Part 2: region enrichment | `missMethyl::goregion` | hg38 | Zhou, GENCODE v41 (passed with `anno =`) |
| Part 3: gene-set enrichment | `missMethyl::gometh` | hg38 | Zhou, GENCODE v41 (passed with `anno =`) |
| Part 3: gene-set enrichment | `methylGSA` | hg38 | Zhou, GENCODE v41 (passed with `FullAnnot =`) |
| Part 3: regulatory-feature enrichment | knowYourCG | hg38, except chromatin states (hg19) | Zhou knowledgebases (Cistrome, Roadmap) |
| Part 3: web tools | EWAS Toolkit, eFORGE | hg19 | Illumina; Roadmap/ENCODE |

The three tables used for annotation, all downloadable from the
[zhou-lab GitHub](https://github.com/zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotationData) are:

- **`EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v41.tsv.gz`** — gene model: gene names,
  transcript biotypes, and signed distance to the nearest TSS.
- **`EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v36.tsv.gz`** — the v36 table additionally
  carries the CpG-island (CGI) relation column we use for island context.
- **`EPIC.hg38.coord.tsv.gz`** — remapped hg38 coordinates. Note this table is
  keyed by genomic position and carries no `probeID` column, so it cannot be
  merged onto results by probe; the v41 manifest above already supplies
  `CpG_chrm`/`CpG_beg`/`CpG_end` and is what we actually join.

Methylation is often a mediator of change. The environment can cause changes to methylation, which subsequently
causes change in gene expression. Methylation sites that cause changes in gene expression are called 
expression quantitative trait methylation sites (eQTMs). So, one additional external layer, the **BIOS cis-eQTM catalog** (whole-blood
methylation→expression links) was added to expand the functional annotation. This helps identify 
which (if any) effector gene may be behind methylation change. I recommend reading more into 
the BIOS eQTM catalog more before using and reporting the results as there are some distinct 
limitations (only 450k methylation array probes were tested, European-ancestry only cohort, original analysis uses hg19 mapping). 
This part of the functional annotation was added to the EWAS Snakemake upon request
from a reviewer for the information. 

::: {.callout-note}

```{r}
#| label: libraries
```

## Part 1 — CpG-level functional annotation {#part-1}

### What annotation resources exist, and which to trust

An EPIC probe ID like `cg16340178` is the Illumina name for a CpG. To interpret
it we need to know **where it lands in the genome** and **what functional
element it tags**. Historically people reached for the hg19 Illumina/minfi
manifest for this, but its coordinates are a genome build behind current
references and its gene mapping is generous (it lists any transcript overlapping
the probe). Zhou's resources supersede it:

| Zhou hg38 table | What it gives | Column(s) we use |
|---|---|---|
| `manifest.gencode.v41` | gencode v41 gene model | `genesUniq`, `transcriptTypes`, `distToTSS` |
| `manifest.gencode.v36` | earlier gene model that also carries CGI relation | `CGIposition` (Island / N_/S_Shore / N_/S_Shelf / open sea) |
| `coord` | remapped hg38 coordinates | `CpG_chrm`, `CpG_beg`, `CpG_end` |
| BIOS cis-eQTM [@bonder2017eqtm] *(external)* | genes whose *expression* tracks the CpG's methylation in whole blood | likely downstream effector gene |

### The annotation join

We start from the BACON-adjusted top-table saved in chapter 06 and left-join the
Zhou tables on probe ID. The v41 gene table can list several TSS distances per
probe (one per transcript); we keep the nearest, which is what defines the
promoter call below.

::: {.callout-note}
## What this section needs
This section starts from `data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz`, written by [chapter 06](06_ewas.qmd). If you
did not run that chapter, fetch the published checkpoint instead:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
./get_data.sh F_ewas_results
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: annotate
# The two Zhou gencode manifests are read straight from the zhou-lab repository.
zhou_epic <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotationData/",
                    "6d176d6e7e56465403d4478a09fe11b983eeb721/Anno/EPIC/")

# 1. EWAS results: the BACON-adjusted toptable from chapter 06
tt <- fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")

# 2. Zhou gencode v41 gene model: gene names, biotypes, signed distance to TSS
v41 <- fread(paste0(zhou_epic, "EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v41.tsv.gz"))
# a probe with several transcripts has several distToTSS values (';'-joined);
# keep the one nearest the TSS — this is what the promoter definition uses
nearest_tss <- function(x) {
  v <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(strsplit(x, ";")[[1]]))
  if (all(is.na(v))) return(NA_real_)
  v[which.min(abs(v))]
}
# one function call per probe over the whole manifest: the slow line here
v41[, distTSS := vapply(distToTSS, nearest_tss, numeric(1))]

# 3. CpG-island relation — only the v36 gene table carries CGIposition
v36 <- fread(paste0(zhou_epic, "EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v36.tsv.gz"),
             select = c("probeID","CGIposition"))
v36[, island := fifelse(is.na(CGIposition) | CGIposition == "", "OpenSea", CGIposition)]

# 4. Join everything on probe ID.
#    all.x = TRUE: every tested CpG stays in the table, annotated or not.
annotated <- tt |>
  merge(v41[, .(probe = probeID, CpG_chrm, CpG_beg, CpG_end,
                genesUniq, transcriptTypes, distTSS)], by = "probe", all.x = TRUE) |>
  merge(v36[, .(probe = probeID, island)], by = "probe", all.x = TRUE)

# 5. Zhou's gene-feature convention: the gene model runs from 1.5 kb upstream of
#    the TSS through the termination site. A probe within +/-1.5 kb of a TSS is
#    promoter-associated; genic but beyond that is gene body; no gene is intergenic.
annotated[, feature := fifelse(is.na(genesUniq) | genesUniq %in% c("", "NA"), "Intergenic",
                        fifelse(!is.na(distTSS) & abs(distTSS) <= 1500, "Promoter", "Gene body"))]
# rank by the BACON p-value
setorder(annotated, bacon.p)

# The deposited table is written a few sections down, after the eQTM columns are
# joined on, so that the file on disk carries every annotation this chapter builds.
```

On our Grady PTSD subset this annotates all **756,251** CpGs with hg38
coordinates and maps **647,034** (85.6%) to at least one gencode v41 gene. The
remaining ~14% are intergenic. This is expected since a large fraction of the EPIC
array deliberately targets enhancers and open sea away from genes.

### The annotated top hits

```{r}
#| label: top10-derive
t10 <- head(annotated, 10)[, .(
  probe, chr = CpG_chrm, pos = CpG_beg,
  # an intergenic probe has no symbol; print a dash rather than NA
  gene = fifelse(is.na(genesUniq) | genesUniq == "", "-", genesUniq),
  distTSS = round(distTSS), feature, island,
  # delta_beta is chapter 06's case−control β difference; ×100 puts it in
  # percentage points, which is how the prose discusses effect sizes
  delta_beta = round(100 * delta_beta, 2),
  bacon_p = signif(bacon.p, 3), bacon_FDR = signif(bacon.adj.P, 3))]
setnames(t10, c("probe","chr","pos","gene","distToTSS","feature","island",
                "\u0394\u03b2 (pp)","BACON p","BACON FDR"))
fwrite(t10, "data/08_annotation/top10_display.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: top10
#| message: false
# written by the `top10-derive` chunk above
t10 <- fread("data/08_annotation/top10_display.csv")
knitr::kable(t10, caption = "Top 10 CpGs by BACON-adjusted p-value, with hg38 coordinates and gene/island context.")
```

Now the list has biological context. The top-ranked CpG **cg15434749** is intergenic
open sea on chr8 with no nearby gencode v41 gene. 
**cg25717994** sits essentially on the `EDNRB` TSS (distToTSS = −12 bp, so
**promoter** by Zhou's ±1.5 kb rule); **cg18321729** tags the `PKM` promoter
(−168 bp); **cg26747885** is in a CpG island (`Island`) at the `SOCS3` TSS
(distToTSS = 455 bp). Four of the top ten fall within 1.5 kb of a
TSS. The trend of top-ranked CpGs being in a promotor region is not seen in this analysis, but may 
appear in a full scale, well-powered EWAS. 
No CpG clears the Bonferroni significance threshold (the top CpG has BACON p ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻⁷ against
a threshold of ≈ 6.6 × 10⁻⁸), and none passes FDR < 0.05 (lowest BACON FDR 0.090). Read this table as
'nominally significant' rather than 'statistically significant'.

In a real study this table is the hand-off point to the enrichment
tools in [Part 3](#part-3) and to comparison against published EWAS catalogs.

### Where the top hits sit relative to genes and islands

A useful sanity check is to compare the
distribution of the top-ranked CpGs across gene features and island context
against the array background. A well-powered signal often enriches in
promoters and island shores.

```{r}
#| label: context-figures
# The two figures below, and the percentages their captions quote. Needs
# `annotated` from the join above; the PNGs it writes are the ones included
# underneath.
TOPN <- 1000
top  <- head(annotated, TOPN)          # `annotated` is already ordered by bacon.p

# One helper for both panels: tabulate a column in the top set and in the whole
# tested set, then convert to a percentage *within* each set, because the two
# sets differ in size by three orders of magnitude and raw counts would not be
# comparable.
mk <- function(col, lev) {
  a <- data.table(set = "Top 1,000",  grp = factor(top[[col]], levels = lev))
  b <- data.table(set = "All tested", grp = factor(annotated[[col]], levels = lev))
  d <- rbind(a, b)[!is.na(grp), .N, by = .(set, grp)]
  d[, pct := 100 * N / sum(N), by = set]
  # top set first, so the series the reader is asking about leads the legend
  d[, set := factor(set, levels = c("Top 1,000", "All tested"))]
  d
}
fd <- mk("feature", c("Promoter", "Gene body", "Intergenic"))
# island levels in genomic order: island, its two shores, its two shelves, then
# everything else — alphabetical order would scramble that
id <- mk("island", c("Island","N_Shore","S_Shore","N_Shelf","S_Shelf","OpenSea"))

ctx_plot <- function(d, xlab) {
  ggplot(d, aes(grp, pct, fill = set)) +
    geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(`Top 1,000`  = "#1A6B75",   # teal
                                 `All tested` = "#B8873F"),  # sand
                      name = NULL) +
    labs(x = xlab, y = "% of CpGs")
}
ggsave("data/08_annotation/08_feature_distribution.png",
       plot = ctx_plot(fd, "gene feature (Zhou gencode v41)"),
       width = 7, height = 3.2, dpi = 300)
ggsave("data/08_annotation/08_island_distribution.png",
       plot = ctx_plot(id, "CpG-island relation (Zhou CGI)"),
       width = 7, height = 3.2, dpi = 300)
```

![Gene-feature context of the top 1,000 CpGs versus all 756,251 tested, using Zhou's promoter (±1.5 kb of TSS) / gene-body / intergenic scheme. The top set leans slightly away from promoters (51.0% vs 52.2%) and toward gene bodies (34.7% vs 33.4%), with intergenic essentially unchanged (14.3% vs 14.4%) — not the direction a real signal usually moves, and a small effect at this sample size.](data/08_annotation/08_feature_distribution.png){#fig-feature width=95%}

![CpG-island context, same comparison, using the Zhou CGI relation. A slight lean toward islands in the top set (19.9% vs 19.2%) and away from open sea (53.7% vs 55.6%). Hold this impression loosely: the formal test in Part 3 (Know Your CpG, another Zhou resource) does *not* find it significant.](data/08_annotation/08_island_distribution.png){#fig-island width=95%}

The distributions move only modestly between the top 1,000 and the background
(@fig-feature, @fig-island). The top-set leans slightly toward islands but not toward promoters, and 
it's not clear if that pattern is more than chance. The bar chart above 
is a useful visual indicator, but not a formal enrichment test, which is covered in [Part 3](#part-3) of 
this chapter.

### The BIOS eQTM layer: methylation that tracks expression

Annotated methylation data often includes a column with the 'nearest gene' to the CpG. This is a useful annotation for 
identifying where in the genome the CpG is physically located and can hint at potential functional impact. For example, 
evidence of methylation at CpG in a promotor region of a gene could indicate a cis-effect between the CpG and expression 
of that gene. However, in reality, DNA sequence is not linear, it has 3-dimensional structure. In 3D space, the 'nearest gene' 
in terms of base-pairs may not be the gene that the methylation site is having an effect on. The answer we really want is 
is whether a CpG actually affects gene expression. The BIOS consortium answered this directly by pairing whole-blood methylation with
RNA-seq in ~3,000 samples and testing every cis CpG–transcript pair, producing a
catalog of **cis-eQTMs** [@bonder2017eqtm]. This information provides the likely
*effector* gene behind a methylation change — which is not necessarily the nearest
gene. 

::: {.callout-note}
## BIOS consortium meQTL catalogs 

The BIOS consortium also provides catalogs for cis- and trans-meQTLs (methylation Quantitative Trait Loci), which provide 
evidence of genetic loci that cause changes to methylation status. This annotation information was not incorporated into 
the snakemake pipeline and how to merge it in will not be covered in this tutorial as it would require lifting over that 
data from hg19 to hg38 and only represents meQTLs for CpGs from the 450k array. If you have both methylation and genetic 
data for your sample, which is often the case, you can perform cis- and trans-meQTL testing yourself. The eQTM relationships 
require having gene expression and methylation data, which is less common and why the effort was made to liftover and update 
the eQTM data from the BIOS consortium. 
:::

The catalogs are keyed on Ensembl gene IDs; the pipeline's
`prepare_bios_eqtm_annotation.R` helper re-maps those to current HGNC symbols for eQTM data. 

::: {.callout-note}
## What this section needs
This section reads `data/08_annotation/bios_eqtm_hgnc_annotated.tsv.gz`, which is committed
to the repository, so there is nothing to fetch. It is the output of a script from the EWAS snakemake pipeline,
`prepare_bios_eqtm_annotation.R`. Please refer to the source code in the
[EWAS repo](https://github.com/krferrier/EWAS) if you'd like to rebuild this file yourself.
:::

```{r}
#| label: eqtm
# Extends `annotated` from the join above. The two files it writes at the end
# are the ones every later section of this chapter reads.

eqtm <- fread("data/08_annotation/bios_eqtm_hgnc_annotated.tsv.gz")

# collapse to one row per CpG: effector gene(s) + strongest eQTM FDR
eq <- eqtm[HGNCName_GRCh38 != "" & !is.na(HGNCName_GRCh38),
           .(BIOS_eQTM_genes  = paste(sort(unique(HGNCName_GRCh38)), collapse = ";"),
             BIOS_eQTM_minFDR = min(as.numeric(FDR), na.rm = TRUE)),
           by = .(probe = SNPName)]

annotated <- merge(annotated, eq, by = "probe", all.x = TRUE)
setorder(annotated, bacon.p)      # merge() re-sorts by the join key; rank it again

# --- what Part 1 hands on -------------------------------------------------
# Export the annotation data as a .csv (as is found in the Zenodo tier H_annotation) and an RDS.
fwrite(annotated, "data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_zhou.csv.gz")
saveRDS(annotated, "data/08_annotation/annotated.rds")
```

On our subset the eQTM layer annotates **10,803 of the 756,251** tested CpGs
(1.4%) with at least one expression-linked effector gene. I will reiterate, there are so few annotations 
because the BIOS eQTM catalog was curated using the 450k methylation array, and not all 
probes used in the 450k array were included in the 850k array. In addition, the BIOS
catalog only keeps pairs at FDR < 0.05. That said, if we filter our results to look our top EWAS hits that
*do* carry an eQTM, we see that the nearest-gene and effector-gene can differ:

```{r}
#| label: eqtm-top-derive
# The twelve rows rendered below: the best-ranked hits that carry an eQTM.
eqd <- annotated[!is.na(BIOS_eQTM_genes)][1:12]
# Is the effector gene also the nearest gene? TRUE when any eQTM gene appears in
# the probe's own (semicolon-separated) gene list. mapply because both sides are
# strings that have to be split row by row.
eqd[, nearest := fifelse(mapply(function(g, e) {
      if (is.na(g) || g == "") return(FALSE)
      any(strsplit(e, ";")[[1]] %in% strsplit(g, ";")[[1]])
    }, genesUniq, BIOS_eQTM_genes), "yes", "no")]
eqdisp <- eqd[, .(probe,
                  nearest_gene = fifelse(is.na(genesUniq) | genesUniq == "", "-", genesUniq),
                  eQTM_gene = BIOS_eQTM_genes, `nearest?` = nearest,
                  eQTM_FDR = signif(BIOS_eQTM_minFDR, 3),
                  bacon_p = signif(bacon.p, 3))]
fwrite(eqdisp, "data/08_annotation/eqtm_display.csv")

# the same hits, untrimmed and with every annotation column, for anyone who
# wants to look further down the ranking than the table below shows
fwrite(annotated[!is.na(BIOS_eQTM_genes)][1:200],
       "data/08_annotation/eqtm_top_hits.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: eqtm-top
#| message: false
# written by the `eqtm-top-derive` chunk above
knitr::kable(fread("data/08_annotation/eqtm_display.csv"),
  caption = "Top EWAS hits (by BACON p) that carry a BIOS cis-eQTM. The 'nearest?' column flags where the expression-linked effector gene is not the nearest gene by distance.")
```

For **cg12218747** the nearest genes are `CBR1-AS1`/`SETD4`, but the
CpG's methylation tracks the expression of **`CBR1`**. For **cg26713179** the nearest gene is
`ZNF766` while the eQTM points at the neighboring **`ZNF528`/`ZNF880`** cluster.
Four of these twelve hits show an effector that differs from the nearest gene.
When reporting results, the effector gene is usually the one people want to know about if the 
information is available. 

## Part 2 — Region-level analysis (DMRs) {#part-2}

### Why look at regions at all

Single-CpG EWAS tests each probe independently, but methylation is not evenly spaced 
throughout the genome, and methylation arrays tend to target CpG islands and gene 
promotor regions where there are likely to be multiple methylation sites close together. 
Methylation sites in close proximity to each other are likely to have the same methylation 
status. A region with several unmethylated CpGs is a stronger biological indicator that is 
an actively expressed region than a single unmethylated CpG, and vice versa for methylated 
regions. This phenomenon in statistics is called spatial autocorrelation. A cluster of five 
or six adjacent CpGs each at p ≈ 10⁻⁴ when tested individually (not reaching statistical significance 
in an EWAS) is, collectively, a statistically significant region. 

### DMR tools

The choice of DMR tool is constrained by **what upstream modeling you did**.

::: {.callout-important}
## comb-p works on summary statistics; DMRcate needs line-level data

**`comb-p`** [@pedersen2012combp] takes only a BED-style formatted file of per-CpG p-values and
coordinates. It never sees the samples or line-level methylation or phenotype data. That means 
it works downstream of *any* EWAS model, however complex. 
If your analysis plan involves stratification and meta-analysis, comb-p is the tool to use. 
This is why the Snakemake pipeline uses **comb-p**.

**`DMRcate`** [@peters2015dmrcate] takes **line-level β/M values plus a single
design formula** and re-fits the model internally to compute a smoothed,
region-level statistic. It is powerful and self-contained, but it **cannot
consume meta-analyzed results** — there is no single design matrix
that represents *"stratify by sex, then inverse-variance meta-analyze."* If you
used the stratified-meta workflow, DMRcate is not an option; if you fit one
pooled model with sex as a covariate, it is.
:::

### Running comb-p on our EWAS results

`comb-p`'s `pipeline` command chains four steps: estimate the spatial
autocorrelation function (ACF) of the p-values, use it to compute
autocorrelation-adjusted regional p-values (the Stouffer–Liptak–Kechris
correction), FDR-correct those, and finally stitch adjacent low-p CpGs into
regions. First we write the BED (this is the pipeline's `make_bed.R`). The
p-values come straight from the chapter 06 BACON fit; the coordinates come from
the same Zhou v8.1 hg38 release the chapter 03 mask came from, so the BED and the
mask cannot drift apart:

::: {.callout-note}
## What this section needs
This section starts from `data/06_ewas.rds`, written by [chapter 06](06_ewas.qmd). If you
did not run that chapter, fetch the published checkpoint instead:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
./get_data.sh F_ewas_results
```

It also needs the probe-order and hg38 coordinate tables from the same Zhou v8.1
release [chapter 03](03_probe_filtering.qmd) used. You do not need to fetch either: the
probe ordering is the copy chapter 03 already committed under `data/`, and the coordinate
table is read directly from the Zhou lab's repository in the chunk below.
:::

```{r}
#| label: make-bed
# This chunk writes the file comb-p needs for input.
tt  <- as.data.table(readRDS("data/06_ewas.rds")$tt)
# The YAME probe order and the coordinate table are two halves of one file pair:
# row i of the coordinate table is the probe named on row i of the ordering
# file, which is why they are assembled side by side and not merged.
# The ordering is the same committed file chapter 03 reads. The coordinate table
# (5 MB) is downloaded from the zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotation repository, pinned to a
# commit so it cannot change underneath the ordering it has to line up with.
ord <- fread("data/EPIC.ordering.tsv.gz", select = "Probe_ID")    # YAME probe order
crd <- fread(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotation/",
                    "e91f9e992cc60f2f52f15c564e359ac6718d4cfd/EPIC/EPIC.hg38.coord.tsv.gz"))
                                                                   # same order, one row per probe
map <- data.table(probe = ord$Probe_ID,
                  CpG_chrm = crd$CpG_chrm, CpG_beg = crd$CpG_beg)

bed <- merge(tt, map, by = "probe")[
  # comb-p walks ordered positions along a chromosome, so keep the assembled
  # chromosomes only: a probe on a scaffold has no neighbors to borrow from
  grepl("^chr([0-9]+|X|Y)$", CpG_chrm),
  # comb-p's column contract: chrom/start/end, the p-value it smooths, and an
  # id it carries through untouched. The '#' on the first name is what makes
  # the header a comment line to the tool.
  .(`#chrom` = CpG_chrm, start = CpG_beg, end = CpG_beg + 2L,
    pvals = bacon.p, cpgid = probe)]
setorder(bed, `#chrom`, start)
fwrite(bed, "data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed", sep = "\t")
```

That writes **756,234** of the 756,251 tested CpGs — the 17 that fall on
unplaced or alt contigs are dropped, because comb-p works on ordered positions
along a chromosome and a scaffold has no neighbors to borrow from.

Then the region detection, with the pipeline's default parameters
(`config.yml`: `min_pvalue = 1e-4`, `window_size = 200`,
`region_filter = 0.05`):

comb-p is a Python tool with its own environment
(`conda env create -f envs/combp.yml`); run the command below in a terminal from the
`tutorial/` folder. Its seven output files are committed under
`data/08_annotation/dmr/`, so the R chunks that follow run whether or not you run it.
`--seed` is the p-value a CpG must reach to start a region, and `--dist` is how far
apart (in bp) neighbouring CpGs can be and still extend it:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
mkdir -p data/08_annotation/dmr
comb-p pipeline \
    --seed 1e-4 \
    --dist 200 \
    --region-filter-p 0.05 \
    -p data/08_annotation/dmr/PTSD_dmr \
    data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed
```

That one command writes seven files, all sharing the `-p` prefix. Nothing
prints the answer to screen, so it is worth knowing which file holds what:

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `PTSD_dmr.args.txt` | the exact invocation, the comb-p version, and the run date — keep this for your methods section |
| `PTSD_dmr.acf.txt` | the fitted autocorrelation function: `lag_min`, `lag_max`, `correlation`, `N`, `p` |
| `PTSD_dmr.slk.bed.gz` | every input CpG with its smoothed regional p: `#chrom`, `start`, `end`, `p` (your input p), `region-p` (SLK-smoothed) |
| `PTSD_dmr.fdr.bed.gz` | the same rows plus `region-q`, the Benjamini–Hochberg correction of `region-p` |
| `PTSD_dmr.regions.bed.gz` | the stitched regions, minimal and headerless: chrom, start, end, `min_p`, `n_probes` |
| `PTSD_dmr.regions-p.bed.gz` | the regions with statistics: `#chrom`, `start`, `end`, `min_p`, `n_probes`, `z_p`, `z_sidak_p` |
| `PTSD_dmr.regions-t.bed` | the regions that pass `--region-filter-p` — here the single region with `z_sidak_p` < 0.05 |

`regions-p.bed.gz` is the file to read: it lists every candidate region with
both the uncorrected and the Šidák-corrected region p. `regions-t.bed` is that
same table filtered down to what survived, which makes it the convenient
endpoint for a pipeline. In this run the two files carry identical columns
because our input BED has no effect-size column for comb-p to carry through.

The ACF step reports short-range autocorrelation in our p-values (correlation
≈ 0.054 out to ~71 bp, p ≈ 2.0 × 10⁻¹²⁸ over 202,078 CpG pairs). Methylation
*is* spatially structured here, as expected. The SLK/FDR steps then propose
two candidate regions, and one of them survives the Šidák correction for the
number of regions tested:

| region (hg38) | n CpGs | `min_p` | `z_sidak_p` |
|---|---|---|---|
| chr6:28,633,493–28,633,701 | 11 | 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁴ | **2.4 × 10⁻¹⁶** |
| chr3:138,608,544–138,608,573 | 2 | 9.3 × 10⁻⁵ | 0.53 |

Those are five of the seven columns in `regions-p.bed.gz` — the three
coordinate columns are collapsed into one here, and `z_p` is omitted (it is the
Šidák-uncorrected region p, 3.3 × 10⁻²⁰ for the chr6 region). The surviving
region sits at **chr6:28.63 Mb, inside the MHC/HLA region**.

::: {.callout-warning}
## `min_p` in the comb-p output is *not* a raw probe p-value
The region above is reported with
`min_p = 8.3 × 10⁻¹⁴` and `z_sidak_p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁶`. Despite the column name,
that `min_p` is not the smallest input p-value in the region: it is the smallest
**Stouffer–Liptak–Kechris–smoothed, FDR-corrected** regional q among the
region's CpGs (the raw SLK p at those same CpGs goes down to 2.2 × 10⁻¹⁹).
Smoothing pools each CpG with its neighbors, so these values are orders of
magnitude below anything in the input: the smallest raw BACON p among the eleven
CpGs is 1.1 × 10⁻⁵, and the smallest anywhere in the BED is
2.0 × 10⁻⁷. Smoothed regional statistics and probe-level statistics are not on
the same scale, and comparing them directly will make a region look far stronger
than the data supporting it.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Set the seed threshold on purpose

`--seed` is the p-value a CpG must reach before comb-p will even *start* a
region there; `--dist` then decides how far the region may extend. The seed is
not a significance threshold for the result — the Šidák-corrected region p is —
so setting it at genome-wide-significance levels defeats the point of doing
region analysis at all. The default of 1 × 10⁻⁴ finds the MHC region
above. If your DMR run comes back empty, you can adjust the seed p-value to
something less stringent, but make sure you have a reason to justify the
p-value you do use!
:::

::: {.callout-tip}
## The MHC is a blood-EWAS landmark

That the strongest regional signal falls in the MHC on chromosome 6. The MHC is
one of the most gene-dense and polymorphic regions of the human genome, and it is
associated with more diseases than any other region [@horton2004mhc]. It also surfaces
in many blood EWAS. It is
simultaneously the region where you should be *most* cautious about SNP-driven
artifacts. We already removed common-SNP-affected sites, but it is possible
that rare variants, structural variants, or undocumented genetic variation is
driving this signal. Further causal inference testing with genetic or gene
expression data can help clarify why we are seeing this signal in the MHC.
:::

```{r}
#| label: fig-dmr
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code for the DMR locus plot"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-cap: "The detected DMR at chr6:28.63 Mb (hg38, Zhou coordinates). Each stem is one CpG within 2.5 kb of the region; the eleven inside the shaded window (teal) are the region comb-p reports, and all eleven are less methylated in cases. Every one sits far below the single-CpG genome-wide threshold (plum line, −log₁₀ p = 7.2), yet together — because they are adjacent and move in the same direction — they reach Šidák-corrected p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁶. This power gain is the entire reason to do region-level analysis."
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

# The strongest comb-p region, by Sidak-corrected p, from the file the command above wrote
lead <- fread("data/08_annotation/dmr/PTSD_dmr.regions-p.bed.gz")[order(z_sidak_p)][1]
lead_chr <- lead[[1]]; lead_start <- lead$start; lead_end <- lead$end

# Every tested CpG within 2.5 kb of the region, with its BACON p-value and hg38 position
ann_loc <- as.data.table(readRDS("data/08_annotation/annotated.rds"))
bonf_line <- -log10(0.05 / nrow(ann_loc))
loc <- ann_loc[CpG_chrm == lead_chr &
               CpG_beg >= lead_start - 2500 & CpG_beg <= lead_end + 2500]
loc[, in_region := CpG_beg >= lead_start & CpG_beg <= lead_end]

ggplot(loc, aes(CpG_beg / 1e6, -log10(bacon.p), colour = in_region)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = lead_start / 1e6, xmax = lead_end / 1e6,
           ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = "#1A6B75", alpha = 0.12) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = CpG_beg / 1e6, y = 0, yend = -log10(bacon.p))) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = bonf_line, colour = "#8C3A4A") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "#1A6B75", `FALSE` = "gray60"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = paste0(lead_chr, " position (Mb, hg38)"),
       y = expression(-log[10]~italic(p)[BACON]))
```

### `ENmix::combp`: the same method, but with R

`comb-p` is a Python command-line tool, which means an extra environment to install for
one step of one chapter. If you would rather stay in R, **`ENmix::combp`**
[@xu2021enmix] implements the same Stouffer–Liptak–Kechris approach, and it takes the
BED we just built with only a column rename. (The same package also offers `ipdmr`
[@xu2020ipdmr], the authors' interval-p-value variant.)

::: {.callout-note}
## What this section needs
This section starts from `data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed`, written by the
`make-bed` chunk above. If you did not run that chunk, fetch the published copy instead:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
./get_data.sh H_annotation
```
:::

```{r}
#| label: enmix-combp
# ENmix's R implementation of the comb-p algorithm. The Python comb-p it is
# compared against below lives in `envs/combp.yml`.
library(ENmix)

bed <- data.table::fread("data/08_annotation/PTSD_ewas_annotated_results.bed")
# ENmix expects its own column names, in this order
data.table::setnames(bed, c("chr", "start", "end", "p", "probe"))
bed <- as.data.frame(bed)          # ENmix wants a plain data.frame
bed$chr <- as.character(bed$chr)

combp(data = bed,
      dist.cutoff = 750,           # must exceed bin.size (see the warning below)
      bin.size    = 310,           # ACF bin width
      seed        = 1e-4,          # FDR threshold for seeding a region
      nCores      = 4,
      region_plot = FALSE, mht_plot = FALSE)

# combp() always writes resu_combp.csv into the working directory; move it
# alongside the other chapter 08 outputs
file.rename("resu_combp.csv", "data/08_annotation/08_enmix_combp.csv")
enmix <- data.table::fread("data/08_annotation/08_enmix_combp.csv")
cat("ENmix regions:", nrow(enmix), "| Sidak < 0.05:", sum(enmix$sidak < 0.05), "\n")
enmix[which.min(enmix$sidak), .(chr, start, end, nprobe, sidak)]
```

It runs in about a minute on our 756,234-row BED and finds the same lead region: a
12-CpG DMR at **chr6:28,633,494–28,633,743**, the MHC-proximal locus command-line
comb-p reports as 11 CpGs at chr6:28,633,493–28,633,701. The probe lists overlap almost
completely; ENmix extends the region by one CpG (`cg12763978`) at the 3′ end.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two ways this differs from the command-line tool:
**`bin.size` must be smaller than `dist.cutoff`.** ENmix builds its autocorrelation bins
by `seq(bin.size, dist.cutoff, bin.size)`, so calling it with the shipped
command-line settings (`--dist 200` with the default `bin.size = 310`) fails with
`wrong sign in 'by' argument` rather than a message naming the problem. The `dist.cutoff
= 750` above is chosen to exceed the default bin width.

**The two implementations do not return the same region count.** With the settings above
ENmix reports **9** candidate regions of which **7** clear Šidák < 0.05, where
command-line comb-p at `--dist 200 --seed 1e-4` reports **2** candidates of which
**1** clears Šidák. Both single out the same chr6 locus as by far the strongest —
ENmix calls 12 CpGs there against comb-p's 11 — but ENmix is much more permissive
about everything else. Some of that is the wider `dist.cutoff`, and some is that ENmix
describes itself as a *modified* comb-p. Treat it as an R-native implementation of the
same idea. Either method is okay, just make sure to report which one you used and its
parameters.
:::

The DMR numbers in this chapter come from the command-line tool at the parameters shown
above, which is what [chapter 07](07_pipeline.qmd)'s pipeline invokes.

### DMRcate: the line-level alternative

If you are using DMRcate, it operates on the M-value matrix directly:

```{.r filename="Generic example, do not run"}
# Schematic only: `M` and `design` are yours to supply. This chapter does not run
# DMRcate: it needs the full M-value matrix and the chapter 06 design in memory,
# and the pipeline's stratified route has no single design matrix to hand it.
library(DMRcate)
# M = CpG x sample matrix; design = model.matrix(~ PTSD + sex + age + cellcounts + SVs)
myannotation <- cpg.annotate("array", M, arraytype = "EPICv1",
                             analysis.type = "differential",
                             design = design, coef = "PTSD")
dmrs <- dmrcate(myannotation, lambda = 1000, C = 2)   # Gaussian-kernel smoothing
results.ranges <- extractRanges(dmrs, genome = "hg19")  # EPICv1 annotation is hg19,
                                                          # unlike this chapter's hg38 regions
```

Note what it requires that comb-p does not: the full `M` matrix in memory and a
single `design`/`coef`. If your EWAS was residualized or meta-analyzed, you
cannot express it as one `coef` here.

### Annotating the DMRs

Once regions exist, the pipeline's `dmr_annotation.R` maps each DMR back to
genes and islands by overlapping its coordinates against three UCSC **hg38** tables:
**refGene**, **cpgIslandExt**, and the **HGNC** gene track. The chunk below downloads
the same three from UCSC. The DMR's constituent CpGs are
looked up by coordinate in the Part 1 annotation table (`annotated.rds`), so each region
carries its probe list and direction of effect. The overlap is a coordinate join — `bedtools intersect` in the pipeline,
or `GenomicRanges::findOverlaps()` if you are staying in R — with no modeling
involved. We run it here for our one region, the eleven CpGs of the
comb-p MHC region at **chr6:28,633,493–28,633,701**:

```{r}
#| label: dmr-annot
library(GenomicRanges)   # GRanges(), IRanges(), overlapsAny(), nearest()
library(jsonlite)        # fromJSON(), for the UCSC API query below

# The comb-p DMR, in hg38: the region with the smallest Sidak-corrected p in the
# regions-p file the comb-p command above wrote
top_dmr <- fread("data/08_annotation/dmr/PTSD_dmr.regions-p.bed.gz")[order(z_sidak_p)][1]
dmr <- GRanges(top_dmr[[1]], IRanges(top_dmr$start, top_dmr$end))

# The same three UCSC hg38 tables the pipeline's fetch_dmr_annotation_cache rule
# downloads. refGene and cpgIslandExt are plain gzipped tables, so fread() reads
# them straight from the UCSC download server.
ucsc <- "https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg38/database/"

# refGene: columns 3-6 are chrom, strand, txStart, txEnd; column 13 is the gene symbol
rg <- fread(paste0(ucsc, "refGene.txt.gz"), header = FALSE, select = c(3, 4, 5, 6, 13),
            col.names = c("chrom", "strand", "txStart", "txEnd", "gene"))
refGene <- GRanges(rg$chrom, IRanges(rg$txStart + 1L, rg$txEnd),   # UCSC starts are 0-based
                   strand = rg$strand, gene = rg$gene)

# cpgIslandExt: columns 2-4 are chrom, chromStart, chromEnd
cgi <- fread(paste0(ucsc, "cpgIslandExt.txt.gz"), header = FALSE, select = 2:4,
             col.names = c("chrom", "chromStart", "chromEnd"))
cpgIslands <- GRanges(cgi$chrom, IRanges(cgi$chromStart + 1L, cgi$chromEnd))

# The HGNC track is a bigBed (the pipeline converts it with bigBedToBed). R's
# bigBed reader cannot parse this file's colour column, so ask the UCSC API for
# the records overlapping the DMR instead (API coordinates are 0-based).
hgnc <- fromJSON(paste0("https://api.genome.ucsc.edu/getData/track?genome=hg38;track=hgnc;",
                        sprintf("chrom=%s;start=%d;end=%d", as.character(seqnames(dmr)),
                                start(dmr) - 1L, end(dmr))))$hgnc

# genes whose transcript lies within 5 kb of the DMR, and the nearest one on each side
near_ref <- refGene[overlapsAny(refGene, dmr + 5000)]
lower    <- refGene[follow(dmr, refGene, ignore.strand = TRUE)]
higher   <- refGene[precede(dmr, refGene, ignore.strand = TRUE)]
length(near_ref)
data.frame(side = c("lower coordinate", "higher coordinate"),
           gene = c(lower$gene, higher$gene),
           distance_bp = c(distance(dmr, lower), distance(dmr, higher)))

hgnc[, c("symbol", "geneName", "locus_type")]

# nearest CpG island: within 2 kb counts as a shore
isl <- cpgIslands[nearest(dmr, cpgIslands)]
distance(dmr, isl)
```

This is a prime example region because **the three annotation sources disagree**, and the
pipeline's default gene table is the one that comes up empty. While often the sources do 
agree, it is not uncommon for annotation disagreements to occur:

```{r}
#| label: dmr-sources-derive
# One row per annotation source: what each names for the DMR. Rows one and two
# come from the UCSC queries in the chunk above; row three from the GENCODE v41
# annotation built in Part 1 (annotated.rds).
ann <- as.data.table(readRDS("data/08_annotation/annotated.rds"))
# the region's CpGs by coordinate, not by a pasted probe list, so the region
# definition lives in one place
reg <- ann[CpG_chrm == as.character(seqnames(dmr)) &
           CpG_beg >= start(dmr) & CpG_beg <= end(dmr)]
setorder(reg, CpG_beg)
stopifnot(nrow(reg) == top_dmr$n_probes)   # the count comb-p reported; fail loudly if the map changed

# every gencode v41 gene the eleven probes are assigned to, de-duplicated
gencode_genes <- paste(sort(unique(unlist(strsplit(reg$genesUniq, ";")))),
                       collapse = ", ")

dmr_src <- data.table(
  `Annotation source` = c("UCSC refGene (pipeline default gene table)",
                          "UCSC HGNC track",
                          "Zhou GENCODE v41 (our probe-level annotation)"),
  names = c(
    if (length(near_ref) == 0)
      sprintf("nothing within \u00b15 kb (nearest %s ~%.0f kb, %s ~%.0f kb)",
              lower$gene, distance(dmr, lower) / 1000, higher$gene, distance(dmr, higher) / 1000)
    else paste(unique(near_ref$gene), collapse = ", "),
    paste0(hgnc$symbol, " (", hgnc$geneName, ", directly overlapping)"),
    paste0(gencode_genes, " (promoter-associated, non-coding)")))
# the second column is labelled with the region's own hg38 coordinates
setnames(dmr_src, "names",
         sprintf("What it names for %s:%s\u2013%s", as.character(seqnames(dmr)),
                 formatC(start(dmr), big.mark = ",", format = "d"),
                 formatC(end(dmr),   big.mark = ",", format = "d")))
fwrite(dmr_src, "data/08_annotation/dmr_source_comparison.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: dmr-sources
#| message: false
# written by the `dmr-sources-derive` chunk above
knitr::kable(fread("data/08_annotation/dmr_source_comparison.csv"),
  caption = "Three hg38 gene annotations, three answers for the same DMR. refGene — the pipeline's default `gene_table` — names nothing nearby; the region only acquires a label from the pseudogene track or from GENCODE.")
```

refGene is a curated set of well-supported transcripts, so a DMR sitting in a
gene-poor stretch of the MHC returns nothing within 5 kb — the nearest curated
genes (ZBED9, LINC00533) are >14 kb away. The HGNC BigBed, which includes
pseudogenes and genes from difficult to map regions, overlaps **COX8CP1** directly, 
and our probe-level GENCODE v41 annotation assigns the CpGs to two non-coding transcripts 
as **promoter** hits.
None of these is "wrong"; they reflect different inclusion criteria. The lesson
for a DMR walkthrough is to **read the coordinates, not just the gene symbol**:
an empty `gene_table` overlap does not mean the region is intergenic junk — here
it is a CpG-island shore over a pseudogene in an immune-gene-dense locus, exactly
the kind of place methylation differences cluster. Our eleven CpGs, all
hypomethylated in cases, look like this:

```{r}
#| label: dmr-cpgs-derive
# The eleven-row table rendered below, and the fuller per-CpG file that backs
# it. Both come from `reg` — the region's CpGs in the Part 1 annotation layer,
# built in the chunk above.
disp <- reg[, .(CpG = probe,
                `hg38 position (chr6)` = formatC(CpG_beg, big.mark = ",", format = "d"),
                # the annotation layer's label is "Promoter (±1.5 kb TSS)";
                # trim the parenthetical so the column stays narrow
                `GENCODE feature` = sub(" \\(.*", "", feature),
                `CGI context` = island,
                # β difference on the 0-1 scale: -0.022 reads as 2.2 points hypo
                `Δβ (case − control)` = round(delta_beta, 3),
                `BACON p` = signif(bacon.p, 3))]
fwrite(disp, "data/08_annotation/dmr_cpg_display.csv")

# the same eleven CpGs with everything the annotation layer knows about them,
# including the transcript list the display table has no room for
full <- reg[, .(probe, CpG_beg, CpG_end, genesUniq, transcriptTypes, distTSS,
                feature, island, BIOS_eQTM_genes,
                delta_beta = round(delta_beta, 4),
                bacon.es   = round(bacon.es, 3),
                bacon.p    = signif(bacon.p, 3))]
fwrite(full, "data/08_annotation/dmr_cpg_annotation.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: dmr-cpgs
#| message: false
# written by the `dmr-cpgs-derive` chunk above
knitr::kable(fread("data/08_annotation/dmr_cpg_display.csv"),
  caption = "The eleven CpGs of the DMR. All fall in the same CpG-island north shore and are hypomethylated in PTSD cases — Δβ between −2.2 and −5.8 percentage points, every one in the same direction. That coherence is what makes a region call meaningful; none of the eleven individual BACON p-values comes close to genome-wide significance.")
```

### From regions to pathways: `goregion`

The gene-set tools in [Part 3](#part-3) take a list of *CpGs*. When your unit of discovery
is a **region**, `missMethyl::goregion` [@phipson2016missmethyl] is the
region-level analog of `gometh`: give it a `GRanges` of your DMRs and it maps
each region to the CpGs it contains, collapses those to genes, and runs the same
probe-number-bias-corrected GO/KEGG test. It is the natural way to ask "are my
comb-p regions collectively enriched for a biological process?"

By default `goregion` (like `gometh` in Part 3) uses **Illumina's hg19** annotation
package to decide which CpGs fall in a region and which genes they belong to, whereas
the rest of this chapter, including the comb-p region itself, uses Wanding Zhou's
**hg38** resources. Both functions accept an annotation of your own through their
`anno` argument, so we build one from the Zhou GENCODE v41 manifest read in Part 1.
missMethyl expects the column names of Illumina's package, so the Zhou columns are
renamed to match:

```{r}
#| label: zhou-anno
# One row per CpG probe with hg38 coordinates. `v41` is the Zhou manifest read in Part 1.
z <- v41[grepl("^cg", probeID) & !is.na(CpG_beg)]
genes <- fifelse(is.na(z$genesUniq), "", z$genesUniq)     # ';'-separated gene names
zhou_anno <- S4Vectors::DataFrame(
  Name   = z$probeID,
  chr    = z$CpG_chrm,
  pos    = z$CpG_beg + 1L,                                # Zhou's starts are 0-based
  strand = fifelse(is.na(z$probe_strand), "*", z$probe_strand),
  UCSC_RefGene_Name = genes,
  # missMethyl wants one gene-region label per gene. It only uses them when you
  # restrict the test to particular regions (genomic.features), which we do not,
  # so a placeholder label is enough.
  UCSC_RefGene_Group = vapply(strsplit(genes, ";"),
                              function(g) paste(rep("gene", length(g)), collapse = ";"), ""),
  row.names = z$probeID)
nrow(zhou_anno)
```

```{r}
#| label: goregion
#| error: true
library(missMethyl)
# The DMR from its eleven CpGs' hg38 positions. `reg` is the region's rows of the
# Part 1 annotation, built in the dmr-sources-derive chunk above.
dmr_gr <- GenomicRanges::reduce(GenomicRanges::GRanges(
  reg$CpG_chrm, IRanges::IRanges(reg$CpG_beg + 1L, width = 2)))

# all.cpg is the tested universe: `tt` is the chapter 06 top-table read in by the
# make-bed chunk above
gr_go <- goregion(dmr_gr, all.cpg = tt$probe, collection = "GO",
                  array.type = "EPIC", anno = zhou_anno)
```

Run on our single MHC DMR, `goregion` **returns an error**: *"There are no genes
annotated to the significant CpGs."*. In Zhou's GENCODE v41 annotation the region's CpGs
are assigned only to two unnamed non-coding genes, which have Ensembl IDs but no gene
symbol. missMethyl can only test genes it can match to an Entrez ID, so there is nothing
to map to a GO term. (Illumina's hg19 annotation gives the same error for this region.) Two lessons
fall out of this:

1. **Enrichment inherits the annotation's gene assignments.** If the annotation
   maps a region to no gene, a gene-centric lens for pathway enrichment will not 
   have anything to query or report. 
2. **`goregion` needs *many* regions to be meaningful.** One region is never an
   "enrichment"; a real DMR analysis feeds it the dozens-to-hundreds of regions
   comb-p or DMRcate returns genome-wide. We show the mechanism here even though
   it doesn't produce a meaningful result so the call is in your toolkit.

## Part 3 — Pathway, trait, and functional enrichment {#part-3}

Annotation names the genes near your hits; **enrichment** asks whether that gene
list is *collectively* over-represented in any biological process, pathway, or
previously reported trait. This is where an EWAS stops being a list of CpGs and
starts pointing at mechanism. Two things make methylation enrichment different
from the gene-expression version you may know:

1. **Probe-number bias.** Genes are not covered evenly on the array — a large
   gene like *PRKG1* carries hundreds of probes, a small one only a handful. A
   naive test that treats "gene has ≥1 significant CpG" as a hit will therefore
   flag long, densely-tiled genes purely because they had more chances to be
   picked. Enrichment for methylation **must** correct for the number of probes
   per gene.
2. **Multiple CpGs map to one gene**, and CpGs in intergenic space map to none.
   The tool has to collapse probes to genes sensibly before testing.

### missMethyl `gometh`: the reproducible, bias-corrected default

`missMethyl::gometh()` (and its generic `gsameth()` for custom gene sets) is the
field-standard R implementation. It maps your significant CpGs to genes, models
the per-gene probe count as the bias covariate, and runs a corrected
hypergeometric test against GO or KEGG [@phipson2016missmethyl]. By default it assigns
CpGs to genes with Illumina's **hg19** EPIC annotation package; passing
`anno = zhou_anno` makes it use the same Zhou **hg38** GENCODE v41 genes as the rest of
this chapter. Enrichment has not 
yet been added to the Snakemake pipeline, but will in a future release.

Normally you would run GO/KEGG enrichment only on the CpGs that reach
epigenome-wide significance. The EWAS of this subset identified none, which leaves nothing
to test, so here we use the top 1,000 CpGs by BACON *p*-value as our "significant
set".

```{r}
#| label: gometh
# The Wallenius test runs over every GO term, so this takes about a minute. The
# RDS written at the end is what the comparison table further down reads.
# `zhou_anno` is the hg38 annotation built in Part 2's zhou-anno chunk.
library(missMethyl)
tt     <- data.table::fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")
all.cpg <- tt$probe                          # tested universe = every CpG you analyzed
sig.cpg <- tt[order(bacon.p)][1:1000]$probe  # your significant set

# GO enrichment, corrected for probes-per-gene. array.type matches your array.
# anno = zhou_anno: genes from Zhou's hg38 GENCODE v41, not Illumina's hg19 default
go <- gometh(sig.cpg = sig.cpg, all.cpg = all.cpg,
             collection = "GO", array.type = "EPIC", anno = zhou_anno)
go <- go[order(go$P.DE), ]

# KEGG is a one-word change
kegg <- gometh(sig.cpg = sig.cpg, all.cpg = all.cpg,
               collection = "KEGG", array.type = "EPIC", anno = zhou_anno)
kegg <- kegg[order(kegg$P.DE), ]

# Both collections in one object. The method comparison below reads `kegg` back
# out of it, and keeping `go` alongside means the GO panel of the figure can be
# redrawn without re-running the test.
saveRDS(list(go = go, kegg = kegg), "data/08_annotation/08_gometh.rds")
```

Two arguments carry all the weight. `all.cpg` is the **full tested set** — it must be
every CpG that survived *your* QC and filtering, not the whole array manifest,
or the test is biased toward whatever your pipeline happened to remove.
Defining "significant" (`sig.cpg`) by a fixed top-*N* (here 1,000) is a teaching
compromise, as noted above.

Run on our teaching subset, the corrected results are:

```{r}
#| label: fig-gometh
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 8
#| fig-cap: "GO and KEGG enrichment of the top 1,000 CpGs by BACON *p*, computed with `gometh` on Zhou's hg38 gene assignments (probe-number–corrected hypergeometric test). The ten leading terms by nominal *P* in each collection, each collection corrected within itself and on its own x axis. Point size and shade show how many genes from the top set fall in the term; solid points pass FDR < 0.05 (dashed line) and hollow points do not. **Nothing survives FDR at n = 86**, the expected outcome when no CpG reaches epigenome-wide significance."
# Drawn the same way as the EWAS pipeline's pathway plot (scripts/plot_enrichment.R
# in github.com/krferrier/EWAS), so this figure and the pipeline's look alike.
library(ggplot2)
library(data.table)

fdr_threshold <- 0.05
# The ten leading terms by nominal p within each collection: GO and KEGG are
# corrected separately, so a pooled top ten would be all GO.
top_terms <- rbind(
  as.data.table(go)[order(P.DE)][1:10, .(collection = "GO", term = TERM, DE, FDR)],
  as.data.table(kegg)[order(P.DE)][1:10, .(collection = "KEGG", term = Description, DE, FDR)])
top_terms[, neg_log10_fdr := -log10(FDR)]
top_terms[, signif := factor(FDR < fdr_threshold, levels = c(TRUE, FALSE))]
# Order each panel by -log10(FDR), then nominal p for ties, so the leading term is on top
top_terms[, term := make.unique(as.character(term), sep = " ")]
top_terms[, term := factor(term, levels = rev(term))]

# An invisible point carrying both significance levels, so the legend always
# explains solid against hollow even when every point falls on one side.
key <- data.table(neg_log10_fdr = top_terms$neg_log10_fdr[1], term = top_terms$term[1],
                  collection = top_terms$collection[1],
                  signif = factor(c(TRUE, FALSE), levels = c(TRUE, FALSE)))

ggplot(top_terms, aes(x = neg_log10_fdr, y = term, size = DE, alpha = DE)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -log10(fdr_threshold), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey55", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = signif), colour = "#1A6B75", stroke = 0.9) +
  geom_point(data = key, aes(x = neg_log10_fdr, y = term, shape = signif),
             size = 0, alpha = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 19, `FALSE` = 1), limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE"),
                     labels = c(sprintf("FDR < %g", fdr_threshold),
                                sprintf("FDR >= %g", fdr_threshold)),
                     drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  scale_alpha(range = c(0.65, 1), guide = "none") +
  scale_size(range = c(1.5, 6), name = "Number of genes") +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2.5, alpha = 1, colour = "#1A6B75"))) +
  # Each collection gets its own x axis, because they are corrected separately
  facet_wrap(~ collection, ncol = 1, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = expression(-log[10] ~ "(FDR)"), y = "Term")
```

The top nominal terms here are zonula adherens (GO:0005915, *P* = 1.6 × 10⁻³), the
catenin-TCF7L2 complex, regulation of syncytium formation by plasma membrane fusion, and
cell-cell adhesion. It is easy to read a cell-adhesion theme into that list, but there is
**no term at FDR < 0.05** in either collection. The smallest FDR in both GO and KEGG is 1 (the top KEGG pathway is Adherens
junction, nominal *P* = 0.0032). This is exactly what enrichment of a **null**
gene list should look like. Reading *this* result as "PTSD methylation remodels
adherens junctions" would be false: with 1,000 arbitrarily-chosen CpGs, a handful of
small gene sets always reach nominal *p* < 0.01 by chance — note that the leading GO
term has only 8 genes in it, 4 of which the top set touched.

### `methylGSA`: the same question, a different bias model

`gometh` is not the only way to correct for the probe-number bias, and the
choice of correction can change the outcome. **`methylGSA`** [@ren2019methylgsa]
offers two alternatives to `gometh`'s Wallenius hypergeometric test. By default it uses
Illumina's **hg19** annotation package; its `FullAnnot` argument takes a CpG-to-gene table
of your own, so we give it the same Zhou **hg38** GENCODE v41 genes `gometh` used. The
three methods below then differ in their statistics, not their gene assignments:

- **`methylglm`** models each gene set with a **logistic regression** in which
  the per-gene number of probes enters as a covariate — a continuous adjustment
  rather than a weighted urn, and it takes the *whole* ranked p-value vector, not
  a hard top-*N* cutoff.
- **`methylRRA`** aggregates the CpG p-values to a per-gene score by **robust
  rank aggregation**, then runs either an over-representation test or a
  **GSEA**-style rank test — no significance cutoff at all.

::: {.callout-note}
## This section runs in its own environment
On the R-only route, `BiocManager` installs `methylGSA` alongside everything else and
there is nothing to do. Conda users need `envs/methylgsa.yml`
(`conda env create -f envs/methylgsa.yml`) because bioconda's newest `methylGSA` build is
for an older R than the rest of the stack. Nothing is shared at run time: the only input
below is the BACON top-table CSV written by chapter 06. Copy the chunk into a script and
run it from the `tutorial/` folder with `conda run -n methylgsa Rscript <script>`; it
writes the three files the comparison chunks below read. Those three files are also
committed to the repository, so the rest of the section runs without this step.
:::

```{r}
#| label: methylgsa
#| eval: false
library(methylGSA)
library(data.table)   # fread()/fwrite()

# This chunk runs in its own R session, so it reads the Zhou v41 manifest itself.
# prepareAnnot() wants one row per CpG: the probe ID and its ';'-separated genes.
v41 <- fread(paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhou-lab/InfiniumAnnotationData/",
                    "6d176d6e7e56465403d4478a09fe11b983eeb721/Anno/EPIC/",
                    "EPIC.hg38.manifest.gencode.v41.tsv.gz"))
cpg2gene  <- v41[grepl("^cg", probeID) & !is.na(genesUniq) & genesUniq != "",
                 .(CpG = probeID, gene = genesUniq)]
FullAnnot <- prepareAnnot(as.data.frame(cpg2gene))

tt <- data.table::fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")
pv <- setNames(tt$bacon.p, tt$probe)          # NAMED vector: names = CpG IDs

# logistic-regression enrichment (bias covariate = probes per gene)
mglm <- methylglm(cpg.pval = pv, FullAnnot = FullAnnot,
                  GS.type = "KEGG", minsize = 10, maxsize = 500)

# GSEA on rank-aggregated per-gene scores. Its p-values come from random
# permutations, so fix the seed to get the same table on every run.
set.seed(20260922)
mrra <- methylRRA(cpg.pval = pv, FullAnnot = FullAnnot, method = "GSEA",
                  GS.type = "KEGG", minsize = 10, maxsize = 500)

# methylGSA looks pathway names up through clusterProfiler, whose older releases
# no longer get human pathway IDs back from KEGG, leaving Description empty. Fill
# any gaps from KEGG's own list of human pathways.
kegg_names <- fread("https://rest.kegg.jp/list/pathway/hsa", header = FALSE,
                    col.names = c("id", "name"))
kegg_names[, `:=`(id = sub("^hsa", "", id), name = sub(" - Homo sapiens \\(human\\)$", "", name))]
fill_names <- function(res) {
  miss <- is.na(res$Description)
  res$Description[miss] <- kegg_names$name[match(res$ID[miss], kegg_names$id)]
  res
}
mglm <- fill_names(mglm)
mrra <- fill_names(mrra)

# Export results
saveRDS(list(methylglm = mglm, methylRRA = mrra),
        "data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa.rds")
glm_top <- head(as.data.table(mglm)[order(pvalue)], 10)[
  , .(Method = "methylglm", KEGG = ID, Pathway = Description, Size, pvalue, padj)]
fwrite(glm_top, "data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_glm_top.csv")
rra_top <- head(as.data.table(mrra)[order(pvalue)], 5)[
  , .(Method = "methylRRA-GSEA", KEGG = ID, Pathway = Description, Size,
      NES, pvalue, padj)]
fwrite(rra_top, "data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_rra_top.csv")
```

We ran all three tools on the **same** BACON top-table, against the **same** KEGG
collection, and recorded both how many pathways each calls significant at
FDR < 0.05 and what each one puts at the top:

```{r}
#| label: gsa-compare-derive
# The comparison table rendered below, rebuilt from the three result files the
# two chunks above write rather than typed out by hand.
g  <- readRDS("data/08_annotation/08_gometh.rds")
kg <- as.data.table(g$kegg, keep.rownames = "ID")[order(P.DE)]
# KEGG ids are zero-padded ("04140"), so they must not be read as integers.
gl <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_glm_top.csv", colClasses = c(KEGG = "character"))
rr <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_rra_top.csv", colClasses = c(KEGG = "character"))
mg <- readRDS("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa.rds")   # full methylglm and methylRRA tables

# A misspelled column name returns NULL, which c() drops without warning; the
# two remaining names would then be recycled down three rows. Check first.
leaders <- c(kg$Description[1], gl$Pathway[1], rr$Pathway[1])
stopifnot(length(leaders) == 3L)

cmp <- data.table(
  Method = c("gometh (Wallenius hypergeometric)",
             "methylglm (logistic regression)",
             "methylRRA-GSEA (rank aggregation)"),
  Input  = c("top 1,000 CpGs vs universe",
             "full named p-value vector",
             "full named p-value vector"),
  `Bias model` = c("probes per gene (Wallenius)",
                   "probe count as covariate",
                   "gene-level RRA score"),
  # The two methylGSA top files hold only their top rows, so the significant
  # counts are taken from the full result tables in 08_methylgsa.rds.
  `KEGG FDR<0.05` = c(sum(kg$FDR < 0.05),
                      sum(mg$methylglm$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
                      sum(mg$methylRRA$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)),
  `Top KEGG pathway` = leaders,
  `Its nominal p` = signif(c(kg$P.DE[1], gl$pvalue[1], rr$pvalue[1]), 3),
  `Its FDR`       = signif(c(kg$FDR[1],  gl$padj[1],   rr$padj[1]),   3)
)
fwrite(cmp, "data/08_annotation/08_gsa_method_comparison.csv")
```

```{r}
#| label: gsa-compare
#| message: false
# written by the `gsa-compare-derive` chunk above
knitr::kable(fread("data/08_annotation/08_gsa_method_comparison.csv"),
  caption = "Three probe-bias corrections, one dataset, one gene annotation (Zhou hg38 GENCODE v41). gometh and methylglm return no KEGG pathway at FDR < 0.05; methylRRA-GSEA returns eight. Each nominates a different pathway as its leader — the ranking, not just the count, depends on the bias model and the input convention.")
```

The three tools use the same genes and the same pathways, and still disagree.
`gometh` and `methylglm` find nothing at FDR < 0.05, with smallest FDRs of 1 and 0.63,
while `methylRRA`-GSEA reports **eight significant pathways**, led by Non-small cell lung
cancer and Pyruvate metabolism (both FDR = 0.026). Each also nominates a
different leader (Adherens junction, Amoebiasis, Non-small cell lung cancer).

Treat those eight pathways methylRRA identifies with caution. `methylRRA`'s GSEA mode uses the full ranking and
no cutoff, so it is the most sensitive of the three *and* the most prone to calling
pathways in a dataset where no single CpG reaches epigenome-wide significance. Its
p-values also come from random permutations: the chunk above fixes the seed so the table
is the same on every render, but without the seed, two otherwise identical runs called
eleven and nine pathways significant. A result that changes with the random seed is not
one to write up on its own; it would need to be confirmed with a different method or in
another cohort.

```{r}
#| label: gsa-rra
#| message: false
# written by the `methylgsa` chunk above
# KEGG ids are zero-padded ("05223"), so read them as text
rra <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_methylgsa_rra_top.csv", colClasses = c(KEGG = "character"))
# NES is only present when the file came from a GSEA run, so take the columns
# that are there instead of failing the render on a missing one
rra_cols <- intersect(c("KEGG", "Pathway", "Size", "NES", "pvalue", "padj"), names(rra))
knitr::kable(rra[, ..rra_cols],
  digits = 4,
  caption = "The five top-ranked methylRRA-GSEA KEGG pathways. All five pass FDR < 0.05 (eight pathways do in total) on a dataset with no epigenome-wide signal, which is the sensitivity/specificity trade-off of a cutoff-free rank test made concrete.")
```

::: {.callout-important}
## The tool is a modeling choice, not a lookup
Report the method **and** its settings, not just "KEGG enrichment." A reviewer
who reruns your CpGs through a different tool will get a different list, and that
is expected — `gometh`, `methylglm`, and `methylRRA` encode different
assumptions about how probe density biases the test. Pick one *a priori* (we
default to `gometh` for its conservative, well-validated behavior), and if you
report a second for sensitivity, say so and show both. Never run all three and
present the one with the prettiest pathway.
:::

### KnowYourCG (KYCG): CpG-centric enrichment on regulatory elements

`gometh` asks a **gene-set** question — it collapses your CpGs to genes and tests
GO/KEGG. But methylation acts through *regulatory elements* — CpG islands,
transcription-factor binding sites, chromatin states, histone marks — and
collapsing to genes throws that resolution away. **KnowYourCG** (KYCG), part of
Zhou's `sesame`/`knowYourCG` ecosystem [@goldberg2025knowyourcg], keeps the CpG
as the unit of analysis and tests your hit set directly against curated
databases of these elements. It is the CpG-centric complement to `gometh`, not a
replacement, and it comes from the same lab as the annotation we used in [Part 1](#part-1).

The knowledgebases are keyed by probe ID, so there are no coordinates to line up, but
they were not all built on the same genome. The CpG-island knowledgebase is derived
from the hg38 manifest's `CGIposition` column (the same source as Part 1's island
context), while the chromatin-state knowledgebase comes from Roadmap chromHMM states
annotated on hg19. The transcription-factor and histone-mark
knowledgebases are hg38: they were built by intersecting ChIP-seq peaks from the
Cistrome Data Browser with the array's CpG coordinates [@goldberg2025knowyourcg], and
Cistrome maps all human data to hg38 [@zheng2019cistrome].

```{r}
#| label: kycg
library(knowYourCG)
library(sesameData)

# Download the EPIC knowledgebases into the ExperimentHub cache. testEnrichment()
# stops with 'either not found or needs to be cached' until this has run once;
# after that it is a no-op.
kycgDataCache()
tt      <- data.table::fread("data/06_ewas_bacon_toptable.csv.gz")
all.cpg <- tt$probe                              # universe = every CpG you tested
sig.cpg <- tt[order(bacon.p)][1:1000]$probe   # your query set

# What CpG-feature databases are available for this platform?
# ALWAYS list first: the catalog names carry datestamps and they change
# between releases. A wrong name fails at load time, not at test time.
listDBGroups("EPIC")           # EPIC knowledgebases: CGI, TFBS, chromHMM, HM, ...

# Cache the databases you want from ExperimentHub, then test.
dbs <- c("KYCG.EPIC.CGI.20210713",               # CpG-island relation
         "KYCG.EPIC.chromHMM.20211020",          # chromatin states
         "KYCG.EPIC.TFBSconsensus.20211013",     # TF binding sites
         "KYCG.EPIC.HMconsensus.20211013")       # histone marks
res <- testEnrichment(query = sig.cpg, databases = dbs,
                      universe = all.cpg, platform = "EPIC")
res <- res[order(res$FDR), ]

# All 863 tested features, one row each: the deposited result table, and the
# input to every KYCG number quoted below.
data.table::fwrite(res, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_results.csv")
```

`testEnrichment` runs a Fisher test of your query CpGs against each database,
using **your** tested set as the universe (the same universe discipline that
matters for `gometh`). The databases are versioned knowledgebases pulled from
ExperimentHub, so the run is reproducible.

The universe is all 756,251 tested CpGs and the query is the same top 1,000 used for
`gometh`, tested against **`r nrow(res)` features** across the four knowledgebases. That number matters for the interpretation below — the four
databases are wildly different sizes.

knowYourCG applies the Benjamini–Hochberg correction **within each knowledgebase**, not
across all 863 features at once. That is a choice with consequences: a feature in the
five-row CpG-island knowledgebase is corrected against four others, while a
transcription-factor feature is corrected against 782. Earlier releases of knowYourCG
corrected across all 863; with that correction the same p-values give 2 significant
features rather than 5, and the difference is the `H1.4`, `H3K9me2` and `8_ZNF/Rpts`
results discussed below. Check which correction your version applies before you report a count.

On our teaching subset KYCG returns **5 features at FDR < 0.05** where `gometh`
returned nothing. The two results are not directly comparable. They ask different
questions: `gometh` collapses CpGs to genes and tests pathways, while KYCG keeps the
CpG as the unit and tests which regulatory elements the CpGs fall in. Their annotations
also differ: `gometh`'s gene assignments here come from Zhou's hg38 GENCODE v41
manifest, whereas KYCG's features come from Zhou's knowledgebases, which are hg38
except for the hg19 chromatin states. The count of 5 also needs care, because KYCG's
feature sets are large and overlap heavily; the callout below works through what
those 5 features do and do not show.

```{r}
#| label: fig-kycg
#| fig-width: 9.5
#| fig-height: 6.6
#| fig-cap: "KYCG enrichment of the top 1,000 CpGs. Each knowledgebase gets its own block along the x axis (number of features tested in brackets), because FDR is corrected within each knowledgebase, not across them. Every over-represented feature (log₂ odds ratio > 0) is drawn, sized by its log₂ odds ratio: solid points pass FDR < 0.05, hollow points do not. The strongest significant feature in each knowledgebase is labelled."
# Drawn the same way as the EWAS pipeline's feature plot (scripts/plot_enrichment.R
# in github.com/krferrier/EWAS), which follows knowYourCG's KYCG_plotEnrichAll.
library(ggplot2)
library(ggrepel)   # geom_text_repel(), labels that avoid the points
library(ggtext)    # element_markdown(), axis labels coloured to match their block
library(data.table)

fdr_threshold <- 0.05
kd <- as.data.table(res)
kd[, kb := sub("^KYCG[.]EPIC[.]", "", sub("[.][0-9]+$", "", group))]
kd <- kd[!is.na(FDR) & is.finite(estimate)]

# Blocks in the pipeline's order: chromatin states and histone marks together,
# then protein binding, then gene context. Alternate groups are shaded.
kb_order <- c("chromHMM", "HMconsensus", "TFBSconsensus", "CGI")
kb_group <- c(chromHMM = 1, HMconsensus = 1, TFBSconsensus = 2, CGI = 3)
kb_cols  <- c(chromHMM = "#B8883E", HMconsensus = "#5B7F95",
              TFBSconsensus = "#1A6B75", CGI = "#8C3A4A")
kd[, kb := factor(kb, levels = kb_order)]
setorder(kd, kb, dbname)

# Each block's width grows with log(number of features), so the 783 TF binding
# sites do not swallow the axis and the 5 CpG-island features stay findable.
n_tested <- table(kd$kb)
kd[, inc := as.numeric((log(2 + n_tested) / n_tested)[as.character(kb)])]
kd[, step := c(0, as.numeric(head(as.character(kb), -1) != tail(as.character(kb), -1)))]
kd[, xpos := cumsum(inc + step)]

blocks <- kd[, .(middle = mean(xpos), beg = min(xpos), end = max(xpos), n = .N), by = kb]
min_w <- 0.006 * diff(range(kd$xpos))
blocks[, half := pmax((end - beg) / 2, min_w)]
pad <- min(diff(blocks$middle)) * 0.12
blocks[, `:=`(rmin = middle - half - pad, rmax = middle + half + pad,
              grp = kb_group[as.character(kb)])]
blocks[, lab := sprintf("<span style='color:%s'>%s (%d)</span>",
                        kb_cols[as.character(kb)], kb, n)]
bands <- blocks[, .(rmin = min(rmin), rmax = max(rmax)), by = grp]
bands[, shade := grp %% 2 == 0]

# Only over-represented features are drawn: the test is one-sided, so a
# depleted feature carries no evidence either way.
pts <- kd[estimate > 0]
pts[, y := -log10(FDR)]
pts[, signif := factor(FDR < fdr_threshold, levels = c(TRUE, FALSE))]
# The strongest significant feature in each knowledgebase gets a label
labs_dt <- pts[signif == "TRUE"][order(-y), head(.SD, 1), by = kb]
y_top <- max(3, max(pts$y) * 1.18)
key <- data.table(xpos = pts$xpos[1], y = pts$y[1],
                  signif = factor(c(TRUE, FALSE), levels = c(TRUE, FALSE)))

ggplot(pts, aes(xpos, y)) +
  geom_rect(data = bands[shade == TRUE], aes(xmin = rmin, xmax = rmax, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf),
            fill = "grey92", colour = NA, alpha = 0.55, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(size = estimate, colour = kb, shape = signif), alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_point(data = key, aes(xpos, y, shape = signif), size = 0, alpha = 0, inherit.aes = FALSE) +
  geom_text_repel(data = labs_dt, aes(label = dbname, colour = kb), size = 2.9,
                  direction = "y", nudge_y = 0.04 * y_top, point.padding = 0.6,
                  box.padding = 0.35, min.segment.length = 0, force = 4, force_pull = 0.3,
                  max.overlaps = Inf, seed = 1, segment.colour = "grey60",
                  segment.size = 0.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = kb_cols, guide = "none") +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 19, `FALSE` = 1), limits = c("TRUE", "FALSE"),
                     labels = c(sprintf("FDR < %g", fdr_threshold),
                                sprintf("FDR >= %g", fdr_threshold)),
                     drop = FALSE, name = NULL) +
  scale_size_continuous(range = c(1.5, 6), name = expression(log[2] ~ "(odds ratio)")) +
  guides(shape = guide_legend(override.aes = list(size = 2.5, alpha = 1, colour = "grey25"))) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = blocks$middle, labels = blocks$lab) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(min(bands$rmin), max(bands$rmax)), ylim = c(0, y_top)) +
  labs(x = "Knowledgebase (features tested)", y = expression(-log[10] ~ "(FDR)")) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), panel.grid.minor.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.x = element_markdown(angle = 40, hjust = 1, vjust = 1))
```

```{r}
#| label: kycg-derive
# This chunk executes: it reads the result table the chunk above wrote and
# derives the three summaries the rest of this section discusses, so none of
# those numbers can drift away from the run that produced them.
k <- fread("data/08_annotation/08_kycg_results.csv")
# testEnrichment names the knowledgebase in `group` and the feature in `dbname`,
# which reads backwards; rename once here
setnames(k, c("group", "dbname"), c("db", "feature"))
# drop the "KYCG.EPIC." prefix and the release datestamp: "CGI", "chromHMM", ...
k[, kb := sub("^KYCG\\.EPIC\\.", "", sub("\\.[0-9]+$", "", db))]

# per-knowledgebase: how much was tested, how much survived, and the leader
ksum <- k[, .(
  `Features tested` = .N,
  `Nominal p<0.05`  = sum(p.value < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  `FDR<0.05`        = sum(FDR < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE),
  `Top feature`     = feature[which.min(FDR)],
  `Top log2(OR)`    = round(estimate[which.min(FDR)], 2),
  `Top FDR`         = signif(min(FDR, na.rm = TRUE), 3)
), by = .(Knowledgebase = kb)][order(-`FDR<0.05`)]
fwrite(ksum, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_db_summary.csv")

# every feature that clears FDR < 0.05, best first
ktop <- k[FDR < 0.05][order(FDR, p.value),
  .(Knowledgebase = kb, Feature = feature,
    `log2(OR)` = round(estimate, 2), `Query CpGs` = overlap,
    `DB size` = nD, p = signif(p.value, 3), FDR = signif(FDR, 3))]
fwrite(ktop, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_top.csv")

# the CGI knowledgebase in full — all five rows, significant or not, because the
# section below reads it as a negative result and needs the near-misses visible
kcgi <- k[kb == "CGI"][order(FDR),
  .(Feature = feature, `log2(OR)` = round(estimate, 2),
    `Query CpGs` = overlap, `DB size` = nD,
    p = signif(p.value, 3), FDR = signif(FDR, 3))]
fwrite(kcgi, "data/08_annotation/08_kycg_cgi.csv")
```

```{r}
  caption = "KYCG results per knowledgebase. The four databases differ in size by two orders of magnitude, and the largest one contributes only one of the significant hits.")
```

Read that table before reading the hits. Three things fall out of it:

- **The 5 hits are not spread evenly** — **1 of 5** comes from
  `TFBSconsensus`, which contributes 783 of the 863 features tested. Three
  come from histone marks, one from chromatin state, and none from CpG-island relation.
- **`8_ZNF/Rpts` (ZNF genes and repeats) is the single chromatin-state hit**
  (log₂OR = 1.96, FDR = 0.039), from only 7 of the 1,000 query CpGs; `1_TssA`
  (active TSS) is not significant (log₂OR = 0.27, FDR = 0.077), consistent with
  the absence of a promoter lean in @fig-feature.
- **The CpG-island knowledgebase has no hit.** Islands are barely enriched
  (log₂OR = 0.06, nominal *p* = 0.30, **FDR = 0.50**) when corrected against the
  other four island categories. The visual island lean in
  @fig-island (19.9% vs 19.2%) is therefore not supported by the formal test.
