::: {.callout-warning}
## 5 significant features is not 5 findings
Before you write these up, check three things that the FDR column alone will not
tell you.

**1. Count the nominal hits.** 122 of 863 features reach nominal *p* < 0.05,
against ~43 expected under the null. That excess is real — the top-1,000 set is
genuinely non-random with respect to regulatory annotation — but it is
distributed across hundreds of overlapping features, not concentrated in a few.

**2. The features are not independent.** The `TFBSconsensus` databases are
consensus binding sites derived from ChIP-seq, and they overlap each other
heavily: the median significant feature covers **1.8%** of the tested universe
(13,338 of 756,251 CpGs). `ZNF335`, `RAG2`, `RBL1`, `L3MBTL2`, and `ING5` each overlap
100,000–117,000 CpGs. Benjamini–Hochberg
assumes independence (or positive dependence); with sets this large and this
correlated, "5 significant" is closer to a handful of distinct signals counted
repeatedly. The more honest description is *one modest enrichment spread over a few
overlapping histone-mark and chromatin-state features*, not 5 separate findings.

**3. Where a feature is tested decides whether it survives.** knowYourCG corrects
within each knowledgebase, so a feature competes only with the others in its own
database. `TFBSconsensus` supplies 111 of the 122 nominal hits (14% of its 783 features,
against 5% expected under the null), yet only one survives, because it is corrected over
783 tests; `HMconsensus` has 8 nominal hits among 60 features and keeps three. Set size
matters too: a larger set needs a smaller effect to reach the same *p*. `H1.4` covers
35,991 CpGs, the largest significant feature, and has the smallest log₂OR (0.61), while
`8_ZNF/Rpts` covers 1,372 and needs a log₂OR of 1.96.
:::

Both tests see the same underlying fact — the top CpGs lean only weakly toward
any annotation — but they differ in what they can resolve.
`gometh` has to collapse CpGs to genes and then test gene sets of a few dozen to
a few hundred members, which at this sample size leaves it no power at all. KYCG
keeps the CpG as the unit and tests sets of tens of thousands, so the same weak
lean becomes formally detectable. They also tell you different things: KYCG tells you more about the epigenetic context of
the CpG, while GO/KEGG tells you more about which biological pathways the methylation
changes might affect. KYCG's overlapping sets also make its hit count a poor guide to how
many independent things you have found.

Run both. Report `gometh`'s null as a null, and report KYCG's 5 features as what
they are — a single, modest enrichment over a few overlapping histone-mark and
chromatin-state features, at a sample size where no individual CpG is convincing.
Most of those features describe repressed or heterochromatic DNA rather than active
promoters: H3K9me2 and the `8_ZNF/Rpts` state (zinc-finger genes and repeats) mark
heterochromatin, and H3K36me2 marks broad intergenic and gene-body domains. That fits the
top set's slight lean away from promoters in @fig-feature.

### EWAS Atlas / EWAS Open Platform Toolkit: the copy-paste web route

When you want a fast look without writing R — or want to cross-reference against
what other studies have already reported — the **EWAS Toolkit**, part of the
EWAS Open Platform (formerly EWAS Atlas) at
[ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/ewas/toolkit](https://ngdc.cncb.ac.cn/ewas/toolkit), takes a
pasted list of CpG probe IDs and runs **seven** enrichment modalities in one
pass [@xiong2022ewasopenplatform; @li2019ewasatlas]. The value is that several
of these draw on curated resources you can't easily reproduce locally:

- **Trait enrichment** — tests your CpG list against the platform's manually
  curated catalog of associations from thousands of published EWAS, using a
  **weighted Fisher's exact test** where each probe is weighted by the number of
  studies reporting that probe–trait association. This is the analysis you
  *can't* reproduce locally without their database, and it is the most useful:
  it tells you whether your hits overlap CpGs already linked to smoking, aging,
  BMI, or a specific disease. 
- **Genomic location enrichment** — assigns each probe to **13 location
  categories** defined relative to gene and CpG island (each probe gets one
  gene-relative and one island-relative category) and tests over-representation
  with a **hypergeometric test** (p-value + odds ratio). This overlaps what
  `knowYourCG` and our own feature/island tables already give you — but note the
  Toolkit's location annotation is **hg19-based** (450K:
  `IlluminaHumanMethylation450kanno.ilmn12.hg19`; EPIC:
  `IlluminaHumanMethylationEPICanno.ilm10b4.hg19`), so it is *not*
  build-consistent with the hg38 annotation we built in [Part 1](#part-1).
- **GO & KEGG enrichment** — implemented on top of `missMethyl::gometh`, so it is
  literally the same probe-bias-corrected test you ran locally; expect
  concordance with your `gometh` result, and read a disagreement as a gene-universe
  difference (the web tool uses the full array as background).
- **Chromatin state & histone modification enrichment** — overlaps your CpGs
  against **Roadmap Epigenomics** data (chromatin state via the core 15-state
  model; 11 histone/accessibility marks: DNase, H2A, H3K27ac, H3K27me3, H3K4me1,
  H3K4me2, H3K4me3, H3K79me2, H3K9ac, H3K9me3, H4K20me1), again by hypergeometric
  test. This is the same *question* `knowYourCG`'s chromHMM/histone databases and
  `eFORGE` answer — a regulatory-context check — but built on hg19 Roadmap tracks.
- **Tissue methylation** — reports whether your CpGs are tissue-specific across
  **31 core tissues** from the EWAS Data Hub (a probe counts as tissue-specific
  when `abs(tau_hyper − tau_hypo) > 0.7`, a cutoff set by permutation). Useful as
  a sanity check that whole-blood hits aren't dominated by a signal that is really
  tissue-of-origin driven.
- **Expression regulation** — reports Pearson correlations between methylation and
  expression across six tissues (brain, colon, kidney, liver, stomach, testis).
  This is the *same idea* as the BIOS eQTM layer we joined in [Part 1](#part-1), but computed
  in solid tissues rather than whole blood — so for a blood EWAS, prefer the BIOS
  blood eQTMs and read this panel as supporting, cross-tissue context.
- **Motif enrichment** — runs **HOMER** on a 500 bp window centered on each CpG to
  find over-represented transcription-factor binding motifs, a lead on which TFs
  might read or be blocked by the methylation change.

The workflow is literally copy-paste: take the `probe` column of your top hits
(or the DMR constituent CpGs), paste into the query box, submit. Practical
notes:

- **It is EPIC/450K-aware but check the array setting**, and paste `cg#########`
  IDs, not coordinates.
- **Mind the genome build.** The location, chromatin-state, and histone panels
  are annotated on **hg19**; the rest of this tutorial is deliberately hg38. That
  is fine for the *categorical* questions these panels answer (is my set enriched
  for enhancers? for island shores?), but don't copy an hg19 coordinate from the
  Toolkit into an hg38 result table.
- **Treat it as a curated cross-check, not a replacement** for the reproducible R
  path. Its trait and tissue panels are the parts you genuinely can't run locally;
  its GO/KEGG and location panels duplicate `gometh`/`knowYourCG`, so use those in
  the pipeline for the record and the Toolkit interactively to mine the catalogs.

### `eFORGE`: is a hit list driven by cell composition?

For a **whole-blood** EWAS the single most important adversarial check is
whether your top CpGs are simply marking a shift in cell-type proportions rather
than a phenotype-specific signal. **`eFORGE`** [@breeze2016eforge] answers this
directly: it takes a set of CpGs (your top hits, or a DMR's constituent probes)
and tests — by matched-background resampling — whether they are
over-represented in cell-type-specific regulatory elements: DNase I
hypersensitive sites and the Roadmap/ENCODE core-15 chromatin states across
~40 blood and other primary cell types.

The result you *want* to see for a well-adjusted blood EWAS is **no strong,
single-cell-type enrichment** — that is evidence your cell-composition
adjustment (chapter 04) did its job. The result that should stop you is a list of 
neutrophil- or T-cell-specific enhancers: a signature that the
"phenotype" effect is really a composition effect that leaked past the model.
Because it works on `cg#########` IDs against pre-built reference panels, `eFORGE`
runs from a web form or the `eForge` R package with no local reference data to
assemble.

::: {.callout-note}
## Why this check matters here specifically
Our subset carries the confounds chapter 05 mapped — cell composition loads
heavily on the leading PCs. An `eFORGE` cell-type enrichment on the top hits is
the natural closing sanity check: it asks the composition question of the
*final* CpG list, after all modeling, in the vocabulary (chromatin states,
DHS) that a reviewer of a blood EWAS will expect to see addressed.
:::

## Other tools worth knowing, and how to choose

No single tool answers every interpretation question. A short map of the
landscape, roughly in the order you'd reach for them:

| Question | Tool | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| GO / KEGG, bias-corrected, reproducible | `missMethyl::gometh` / `gsameth` | Default gene-set test. `gsameth` takes any custom gene-set list (e.g. MSigDB Hallmark). |
| CpG-centric enrichment on regulatory elements | `knowYourCG::testEnrichment` | CGI, TFBS, chromatin state, histone marks — tests CpGs directly, no gene collapse. From the same lab as the Zhou annotation; hg38 except the chromHMM knowledgebase (hg19). |
| Region-level GO enrichment from DMRs | `missMethyl::goregion` | Feeds comb-p/DMRcate regions in directly, correcting for probes-per-region. |
| "Has this CpG been linked to a trait before?" | EWAS Toolkit / EWAS Catalog / MRC-IEU EWAS Catalog | Curated look-ups; the fastest external validation. |
| Broad gene-set / pathway diagrams, no bias model | ShinyGO, g:Profiler, Enrichr, GREAT | Built for gene lists generally; **do not** correct for methylation probe bias, so feed them a gene list you already trust, not raw CpG hits. |
| Cell-type / tissue enrichment (is a hit driven by composition?) | `eFORGE`, LOLA | Tests whether your CpGs cluster in cell-type-specific regulatory elements — a direct check on residual confounding. |
| Chromatin-state / enhancer context | Roadmap/ENCODE overlaps via LOLA or `annotatr` | Places hits in enhancers, promoters, and TF-binding regions. |
| Causal direction (does methylation *cause* the phenotype?) | Mendelian randomization with mQTLs (e.g. GoDMC) | The rigorous follow-up when a hit is real; well beyond a single EWAS. |
| "Is my phenotype associated with epigenetic *age*?" | Epigenetic clocks: `methylclock`, Horvath [@horvath2013clock] / Hannum [@hannum2013clock] predictors | A composite outcome computed from a fixed CpG set, not an enrichment of *your* hits. Fit it as a separate phenotype-level analysis; don't read it off your EWAS table. |


## Interpreting the result: a short checklist

Before writing "our EWAS implicates pathway X," walk through:

1. **Did anything survive FDR at the CpG level?** If not (as here), say so plainly
   and treat enrichment as hypothesis-generating, not confirmatory.
2. **Is the enrichment robust?** Re-run with the full-array
   background vs your filtered set; a term that only appears with a permissive
   background is fragile.
3. **Does trait enrichment corroborate the biology?** Overlap with previously
   reported CpGs is stronger evidence than a lone GO term.
4. **Could composition explain it?** Check with `eFORGE` or by confirming your
   cell-count adjustment (chapter 04) held.
5. **Is the direction consistent?** Hyper- vs hypo-methylation across a region or
   pathway should tell a coherent story; scattered directions suggest noise.
6. **How big are the feature sets, and do they overlap?** A CpG-centric test on
   very large, correlated annotation sets will produce many significant features
   from one underlying signal. Count distinct signals, not rows.
7. **Are the hits you are annotating stratum-specific?** If they came from a
   stratified meta-analysis, look up the per-stratum statistics first (notebook
   [07](07_pipeline.qmd)) — annotating a CpG that only one arm supports is
   annotating one stratum's noise.

::: {.callout-important}
## Two caveats this walkthrough inherits, and you should carry forward
Everything in this chapter is downstream of choices made in notebooks 05–07, and
two of them limit how far the annotation can be pushed.

**The surrogate variables were estimated on the whole cohort.** When those same
SVs are used inside a single-sex stratum they still carry sex-defined structure,
because they were built to describe variation across both sexes. A cleanly
stratified analysis would re-estimate SVs within each stratum — which the
Snakemake pipeline is not currently set up to do (notebook
[07](07_pipeline.qmd)). Treat stratum-specific hits as provisional for this
reason alone.

**Per-stratum power is very low.** The stratified arms fit 26 design columns (the
full model without sex) to 44 and 42 samples, leaving 18 and 16 residual degrees of
freedom. That is enough to fit the model and not enough to estimate small effects
precisely.
:::

## Summary

- **Annotation makes probe IDs biologically interpretable.** Take coordinates, gene model,
  and CpG-island relation all from **one genome build annotation set**; don't mix 
  annotations built from hg19 with those from hg38. The BIOS eQTM catalog provides some 
  annotation for likely effector genes, which can differ from the nearest gene. 
- **Region analysis recovers signal that single-CpG testing misses** by
  leveraging the spatial correlation of methylation. On our subset an
  11-CpG MHC cluster reaches Šidák p = 2.4 × 10⁻¹⁶ while none of its CpGs comes
  close to the single-CpG EWAS significance threshold.
- **Match the DMR tool to your upstream model.** `comb-p` runs on summary
  statistics and therefore works after stratified meta-analysis. `DMRcate` needs line-level data and one design formula, so it
  cannot consume meta-analyzed results.
- **Run enrichment multiple ways.** `missMethyl::gometh` for
  reproducible, probe-bias-corrected **gene-set** (GO/KEGG) tests;
  `knowYourCG::testEnrichment` for **CpG-centric** tests against regulatory-element
  databases (CGI, TFBS, chromatin state); and the EWAS Toolkit for the **trait**
  catalog you can't reproduce locally. Read the **FDR** column, not the nominal
  *p*, and always feed the tool your real tested CpG-set. On this subset, with
  all three gene-set tools given the same Zhou hg38 genes, `gometh` and `methylglm`
  return **nothing** at FDR < 0.05 and `methylRRA`-GSEA returns eight pathways whose
  count changes with the permutation seed. KYCG returns **5 of 863** regulatory
  features — a difference driven as much by set size and how the tests are corrected as by biology, and one whose
  honest reading is a single modest enrichment over a few overlapping histone-mark
  and chromatin-state features rather than 5 discoveries.
- Real outputs from this notebook —
  `PTSD_ewas_annotated_zhou.csv.gz` (full Zhou-annotated table), the KYCG results
  table, and the comb-p DMR files — are the biological deliverables of the whole
  tutorial. The single-CpG hits don't survive correction on this teaching subset,
  which is the expected result at n = 86.

::: {.callout-note}
## Other arrays

Zhou publishes the same
hg38 annotation set for every array — swap `EPIC` for `HM450` or
`EPICv2` in the manifest/gene/SNP filenames and in the `platform`/`array.type`
arguments to `testEnrichment`/`gometh`. The comb-p and DMRcate calls are
unchanged apart from the `arraytype` argument.
:::
